chief_complaint: feeling full after eating only a few bites and burning upper stomach pain for 4 months
hpi_details: 4-month history of persistent gnawing epigastric pain that is not relieved by over-the-counter antacids. Experiences early satiety after eating less than half her normal portion, persistent mild nausea, and distaste for meat. Has lost 7kg over the past 4 months. Denies dysphagia or haematemesis.
ideas: thinks she has a stomach ulcer from chronic stress and eating pickled foods
concerns: worried about the rapid weight loss and lack of energy to play with her grandchildren
expectations: wants a stronger acid-suppression pill that will restore her appetite
pmh: H. pylori eradication therapy attempted 12 years ago (unsure of eradication confirmation), mild hypertension
medications: losartan 50mg OD, famotidine 20mg BD over-the-counter with no relief
social_hx: non-smoker, drinks green tea daily, emigrated from Japan 30 years ago, diet high in salted/preserved foods

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Gastric Adenocarcinoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Urgent two-week-wait referral for diagnostic gastroscopy with biopsy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: feeling full after eating only a few bites and burning upper stomach pain for 4 months

Key HPI features: 4-month history of persistent gnawing epigastric pain that is not relieved by over-the-counter antacids. Experiences early satiety after eating less than half her normal portion, persistent mild nausea, and distaste for meat. Has lost 7kg over the past 4 months. Denies dysphagia or haematemesis.

Objective/Exam findings: Abdominal exam: palpate for epigastric mass, check for left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (Virchow's node) or umbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule). Bloods: FBC (microcytic anaemia), iron panel, LFTs. Urgent upper GI endoscopy (OGD) with multiple biopsies of suspicious lesions.
Relevant background/PMH: H. pylori eradication therapy attempted 12 years ago (unsure of eradication confirmation), mild hypertension
Current medications: losartan 50mg OD, famotidine 20mg BD over-the-counter with no relief
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Gastric Adenocarcinoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Refractory benign peptic ulcer disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Unintentional weight loss with early satiety and pain unresponsive to acid suppression.
management_principles: Urgent two-week-wait referral for diagnostic gastroscopy with biopsy
Staging CT abdomen/thorax if malignant features noted on endoscopy
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 61F with history of H. pylori presents with 4-month epigastric pain refractory to H2 blockers, early satiety, food aversion, and 7kg weight loss.
reference_soap.objective: Abdominal exam: palpate for epigastric mass, check for left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (Virchow's node) or umbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule). Bloods: FBC (microcytic anaemia), iron panel, LFTs. Urgent upper GI endoscopy (OGD) with multiple biopsies of suspicious lesions.
reference_soap.assessment: Gastric adenocarcinoma until proven otherwise. DDx: refractory benign peptic ulcer disease, gastric lymphoma (MALT), chronic atrophic gastritis.
reference_soap.plan: Urgent two-week-wait referral for diagnostic gastroscopy with biopsy. Staging CT abdomen/thorax if malignant features noted on endoscopy. Nutritional support consultation.

learning_objectives: Identify epidemiological and dietary risk factors for gastric malignancy including H. pylori history and preserved foods
Recognise subtle upper GI red flags: early satiety, unexplained weight loss, new-onset dyspepsia over age 55
Assess for metastatic signs on physical examination (Virchow's node, Sister Mary Joseph nodule)
Guide the patient from seeking empirical symptomatic relief toward urgent diagnostic gastroscopy

teaching.one_liner: A malignant tumour in the stomach lining causes persistent epigastric pain, early fullness after only a few bites, and steady weight loss that doesn't respond to acid-suppressing medicine.
red_flags: Unintentional weight loss with early satiety and pain unresponsive to acid suppression

must_ask.say: Do you feel full after only a few bites, less than you used to eat?
Have the antacid tablets given you any relief at all?
How much weight have you lost, and how quickly?
Have you gone off eating meat, or noticed foods taste different?
Have you ever been treated for an H. pylori infection or a stomach ulcer?
Have you vomited any blood, or noticed black, tarry stools?
What kind of food do you eat regularly — a lot of salted or pickled food?
